script.opening: (Holding Alfie, visibly exhausted, voice cracking.) "He brings his milk back up after nearly every feed, sometimes loads of it, and then he cries and arches his back. I'm shattered — I'm up all night. My friend's baby was put on a medicine for reflux. Please, can you just give Alfie something to stop it? I can't keep doing this."

facts.text: Bottle-fed formula. "Every few hours, day and night" — about 150 ml every 2–3 hours, often finishes the bottle and wants more (about 1.1 litres a day). "I wind him but it doesn't seem to make much difference."
"It just comes up — never shooting, never green. No blood." Mouthfuls, sometimes "a big splash", mostly within half an hour of a feed. Started at about 3 weeks.
"He feeds fine, he's hungry. Loads of wet nappies. Nothing odd in his poo" — yellow, soft, no blood or mucus. Not refusing feeds.
"No, his skin's fine. He's never been ill." No eczema, no wheeze, no fevers, no cough with feeds. Crying in the evenings for an hour or two; settles when held upright.
"Here — the health visitor's been weighing him" (holds the red book to the camera): birth 3.4 kg on the 50th centile; last week 6.2 kg, still on the 50th.
Term, normal delivery, no special care. Immunisations up to date. No medicines. No family allergies except Dad's hay fever.
If asked about low mood or loss of interest: "Mostly I'm just so tired. I don't know if it's more than that." Enjoys moments with Alfie. Cries most days. No thoughts of harming herself or the baby.
"Not as much as I need." Partner, Liam, back at work; her mum lives 2 hours away. First baby. Mum is 24.

Tearful and desperate. If asked what worries her: "That he's in pain and I'm not helping him. That I'm doing something wrong. Everyone else seems to cope." Pushes for medicine: "But what about the medicine my friend's baby had?" and "So there's nothing?" Feels better with practical feeding changes and support: "That sounds more doable than I thought."

ice.ideas: "He's got reflux and needs a medicine like my friend's baby."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — that Alfie is in pain and she's failing him; exhaustion and low mood she hasn't told anyone about; feeling everyone else copes better.

cues: "I can't keep doing this." — invites asking how she is.
"He finishes the bottle and wants more." — possible over-feeding, if feeds are explored.
"Everyone else seems to cope." — comparison and guilt.

checkpoints.text: Recognises uncomplicated gastro-oesophageal reflux as NORMAL and common in a thriving baby (improving with age/weaning) — but only reassures AFTER assessing feeding, growth and red flags

Assesses FEEDING (volume/frequency — over-feeding, technique, winding, breast/bottle) and PLOTS WEIGHT on a growth chart (red-book or health-visitor weights), arranging for a feed to be observed face to face since this is a video consultation

EXCLUDES red flags: pyloric stenosis (projectile vomiting, hungry, weight loss, 2–8 weeks), bile-stained vomiting (surgical), GORD complications (faltering growth, feeding aversion, back-arching, haematemesis), cow’s-milk protein allergy (eczema, blood/mucus in stool, atopy), serious illness/dehydration

Gives CONSERVATIVE first-line management (NICE NG1 stepwise: review/avoid over-feeding, smaller more frequent feeds, winding, thickened formula if bottle-fed, then an alginate alone if that fails — never with a thickener; back to sleep, no positional management when sleeping) and AVOIDS reflexive PPI/H2 for uncomplicated reflux or visible regurgitation alone

Considers a CMPA trial (maternal dairy exclusion if breastfeeding / hydrolysed formula) or an alginate trial only after the feeding steps (never with a thickener) and where the history fits — escalating appropriately, not reflexively
VALIDATES and SUPPORTS the exhausted parent — acknowledges sleep deprivation, screens MATERNAL MOOD, checks support, signposts help — rather than dismissing her with "it’s just reflux"
Reads the plea as exhaustion/helplessness, reassures she is not failing, and addresses comparison pressure without unnecessary medicalisation

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting urgent review (projectile/bile vomiting, poor feeding, dehydration, faltering growth), conservative plan with review, maternal support and health-visitor involvement — baby and mother both cared for

worked.txt: "Before anything — this sounds exhausting, and being up all night with a crying, sicky baby is genuinely hard. You’re not failing; you’ve done the right thing bringing him. Let me check him over and we’ll make a plan together."

"Can you tell me how much and how often he feeds, and how you wind him? … Have you got his red book? Let me plot his recent weights. … He’s growing beautifully, which is really reassuring — it tells me he’s thriving despite the mess."

"A few important checks: is the vomit ever forceful and shooting across the room, or green? Is there blood, any eczema or blood in his nappies? … None of that — good, that rules out the things I’d worry about."

"So this is normal baby reflux — his food-pipe valve is just immature, and it almost always settles by his first birthday. Let’s try smaller, more frequent feeds, keeping the total the same, and good winding; I’ll ask the health visitor to watch a feed and weigh him this week. Often that’s enough. Keep putting him down to sleep flat on his back."

"I know your friend’s baby had a medicine, but the acid-suppressing ones don’t actually help simple bringing-up of milk and aren’t recommended for it. If he were distressed feeding or not growing, we’d think again — but he’s thriving."

"How are YOU doing in yourself, with the sleep and everything? … Let’s get the health visitor involved and look at some support. Come back if he vomits forcefully or green, refuses feeds, isn’t weeing, or stops gaining weight. And come back for you, too — not just him."

f.learning: Uncomplicated gastro-oesophageal reflux (posseting/regurgitation) is normal and very common in babies because the lower oesophageal sphincter is immature, affecting about 40% of infants, usually starting before 8 weeks and resolving in about 90% before 1 year (NICE NG1) — in a thriving, otherwise well baby it is a laundry problem, not a disease — but reassurance must follow proper assessment. Assess feeding (volume and frequency, since over-feeding is common and worsens reflux, plus technique, winding and breast vs bottle) and plot the weight on a growth chart (red-book or health-visitor weights), arranging an observed feed face to face because a video call cannot replace it, because much "reflux" improves with feeding adjustments alone. Exclude the red flags that mimic or complicate reflux: pyloric stenosis (forceful projectile vomiting, hunger after vomiting, weight loss/dehydration, typically 2–8 weeks and commoner in firstborn males — a surgical emergency); bile-stained green vomiting (urgent surgical obstruction); GORD with complications (faltering growth, marked feeding aversion, distressed back-arching/Sandifer’s, haematemesis, apnoea); cow’s-milk protein allergy (eczema, blood/mucus in stools, other atopy — consider maternal dairy exclusion if breastfeeding or a hydrolysed formula); and serious illness/dehydration. For uncomplicated reflux, first-line management is conservative and stepwise (NICE NG1): avoid over-feeding, offer smaller more frequent feeds with the same daily total and ensure good winding, then for formula-fed infants a thickened formula, and only if that fails stop the thickener and try an alginate for 1–2 weeks (breastfed infants: a breastfeeding assessment first, then an alginate trial) — never a thickener and an alginate together, and no positional management for sleeping infants (back to sleep) — while AVOIDING reflexive acid suppression, as PPIs/H2 blockers are not recommended for overt regurgitation alone (NG1 allows a 4-week trial only for unexplained feeding difficulty, distressed behaviour or faltering growth). Crucially, support the exhausted parent: validate how hard it is, acknowledge sleep deprivation, screen maternal mood for postnatal depression/anxiety (NICE CG192 questions), check support and signpost help — caring for the frazzled parent is caring for the baby. The hidden agenda is a plea born of exhaustion and helplessness as much as a request for medication; assess and reassure properly, give practical help, support her, and avoid both dismissal and unnecessary medicalisation.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG1 (2015, updated 2019) — Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in children and young people · NICE CG116 — Food allergy in under 19s · NICE CG192 — Antenatal and postnatal mental health · BNFC
knowledge.summary: Regurgitation in a thriving, well baby is gastro-oesophageal reflux, not disease. Assess feeding, growth and red flags, then reassure and adjust feeds. Acid suppression is not for regurgitation alone. The exhausted parent is part of the consultation.

points.t: NICE NG1: regurgitation affects about 40% of infants, usually starts before 8 weeks, becomes less frequent with time and resolves in about 90% before 1 year. It does not usually need investigation or treatment.

points.h: Red flags that change the diagnosis
points.t: NICE NG1: bile-stained (green) or blood-stained vomit, projectile vomiting in the first 2 months (pyloric stenosis), abdominal distension, onset after 6 months, bulging fontanelle, fever or systemic illness, blood in the stool, faltering growth.

NICE NG1: review the feeding history; reduce volumes only if excessive for weight; try smaller, more frequent feeds with the same total daily amount; then a thickened formula; then stop the thickener and try an alginate for 1 to 2 weeks.
NICE NG1: a breastfeeding assessment by someone with the right training first; consider an alginate trial for 1 to 2 weeks if distress continues. Do not use a thickener and an alginate together.

NICE NG1: do not offer a PPI or H2 receptor antagonist for overt regurgitation alone. Consider a 4-week trial only with unexplained feeding difficulty, distressed behaviour or faltering growth, and stop it if there is no response. Do not advise positional management for sleeping infants — back to sleep.

NICE CG116: consider non-IgE-mediated cow’s milk allergy if there is eczema, diarrhoea or blood or mucus in the stool alongside reflux. NICE CG192: ask about the parent’s mood using the depression identification questions.

dg.d: Open question; noticed the exhausted parent on screen; let her describe the feeds, crying and back-arching.
Sleep deprivation, support at home, comparison with a friend’s baby, feeling of failing.
Red-book weights plotted; observed on video; face-to-face review if any doubt; no investigations for uncomplicated reflux.
GOR versus GORD, pyloric stenosis, obstruction, cow’s milk allergy, infection and overfeeding.
Projectile, bilious or bloody vomit, feed refusal, hydration, fever, faltering growth, eczema or blood in stools.
Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux in a thriving infant; possible maternal exhaustion or low mood to explore.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: NG1 stepwise feeding measures, alginate only after that and not with a thickener, no PPI for regurgitation alone, back-to-sleep advice.
Maternal mood screened with CG192 questions; health-visitor involvement; separate appointment for the mother.
999 and same-day features named; growth monitoring; review for the mother in two weeks; crisis advice.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I can’t keep doing this” and “I’m doing something wrong” and moved to the mother’s mood.
Idea (reflux needs medicine); concern (he is in pain, she is failing); expectation (a prescription).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — that Alfie is in pain and she's failing him; exhaustion and low mood she hasn't told anyone about; feeling everyone else copes better — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, and hello Alfie. Thank you for calling — you look worn out. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Open question that notices the parent’s state

model.text: He brings his milk back after nearly every feed, sometimes loads, then he cries and arches his back. I’m up all night. My friend’s baby got a reflux medicine. Please can you give him something? I can’t keep doing this.

That sounds really hard, and you’ve done the right thing calling. I want to make sure Alfie’s alright and that you get some help too. Can I ask some questions about his feeding and growth, then we’ll talk about what will help?
model.why: Validates, and sets an agenda that includes the mother

model.text: Okay.
Tell me about his feeds — how often, how much, and how you wind him.
model.why: Feeding history comes first in NG1

model.text: Every few hours, day and night. I wind him but it doesn’t seem to make much difference.
When the milk comes up, does it just flow out of his mouth, or is it forceful — shooting across the room? Has it ever been green, or had blood in it?
model.why: Screens for pyloric stenosis, obstruction and haematemesis

model.text: It just comes up — never shooting, never green. No blood.
Does he feed willingly, or has he started refusing feeds? And what are his nappies like — plenty of wet ones, and any blood or mucus in his poo?
model.why: Feeding aversion, hydration and cow’s milk allergy features

model.text: He feeds fine, he’s hungry. Loads of wet nappies. Nothing odd in his poo.
Any rashes or dry, itchy patches of skin? Any fevers, or times he’s floppy or hard to wake?
model.why: Eczema as an allergy cue and signs of serious illness

model.text: No, his skin’s fine. He’s never been ill.
Have you got his red book? I’d like to see his recent weights so we can check how he’s growing.
model.why: Growth trajectory is the key discriminator between GOR and GORD

model.text: Here — the health visitor’s been weighing him.
Thank you. … He’s following his line nicely. That really matters — it tells me he’s getting plenty of milk despite what comes back.
What’s been worrying you most about it?
That he’s in pain and I’m not helping him. That I’m doing something wrong. Everyone else seems to cope.

You’re not doing anything wrong — lots of parents feel exactly this. Can I ask about you for a moment? Over the last month, have you often felt down, depressed or hopeless, or had little interest or pleasure in doing things?
model.why: Responds to the cue of failure and screens maternal mood (CG192 questions)

model.text: Mostly I’m just so tired. I don’t know if it’s more than that.
Thank you for telling me. I’d like to come back to that properly, because you matter here too. Do you have anyone helping at home at the moment?
model.why: Takes the mood answer seriously and explores support

model.text: Not as much as I need.

Here’s what I think. Alfie has reflux — the valve at the top of his stomach is still immature, so milk comes back up. Around four in ten babies do this. He’s growing well, feeding well, and none of the worrying signs are there. It usually gets better over the coming months, and most babies are through it by their first birthday.
model.why: Explains physiological GOR with the NG1 natural history

model.text: But what about the medicine my friend’s baby had?

I understand why you’d want that. The acid medicines don’t stop milk coming back up — they only change how acidic it is — and the national guidance says not to use them for bringing up milk on its own, because they have side effects without helping. If he were refusing feeds, very distressed despite the other changes, or not growing, we’d think again.
model.why: Declines the PPI with a clear reason and a conditional plan

model.text: So there’s nothing?

There’s quite a lot. If he’s on bottles, we try smaller feeds more often, keeping the total the same, and if that doesn’t help, a thickened feed. If he’s breastfed, I’d like the health visitor or a feeding specialist to watch a feed. And if he stays very unsettled after that, a short trial of an alginate like Gaviscon Infant is reasonable — just not together with a thickener.
model.why: NG1 stepwise plan for both feeding methods without inventing which applies

model.text: Okay. That sounds more doable than I thought.
Good. We’ll start with the feed review and smaller, more frequent feeds. Keep putting him down to sleep on his back — raising the cot or sleeping him on his front isn’t safe and doesn’t help.
model.why: Safe sleep advice; avoids positional treatment in sleep

model.text: Okay.

And for you: I’d like the health visitor to visit this week, and I’d like to see you — just you — in a couple of weeks to talk about how you’re sleeping and feeling. If you ever feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself or Alfie, call us or 111 straight away.
model.why: Treats the mother as a patient too, with a specific safety-net

model.text: That would help. Thank you.

For Alfie, call 999 if he’s floppy, hard to wake or struggling to breathe. Contact us the same day if the vomit becomes forceful or green, there’s blood, he refuses feeds, has far fewer wet nappies, or has a fever. And bring him back if he stops following his growth line.
model.why: Specific red flags for obstruction, pyloric stenosis, dehydration and illness

model.text: Forceful, green, blood, not feeding, dry nappies.

Exactly. So: it’s common reflux, he’s thriving, we adjust feeds rather than use acid medicine, the health visitor comes this week, and I see you in two weeks. Does that feel like a plan you can manage?
Yes. I feel a bit less like I’m failing him.

social.t: Exhaustion reduces a parent’s ability to cope and raises risk; practical support at home and from the health visitor is part of the treatment.
Friends’ experiences and online forums drive requests for medicine; acknowledge them rather than dismiss them.

legal.t: A crying baby with an exhausted parent is a recognised risk situation for abusive head trauma. Ask about coping, give advice on what to do if overwhelmed, and act on any concern.

professional.t: NICE CG192: at contacts in the first postnatal year, consider asking the depression identification questions. Offer her a separate appointment and record the discussion.
Declining an unhelpful medicine while offering a clear alternative plan is good practice (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

community.t: The health visitor can review feeding and growth and assess maternal wellbeing; infant-feeding specialists support breastfeeding assessment. Cry-sis offers a helpline for parents of crying babies.

Blood in vomit or stool, distension, bulging fontanelle, fever or a floppy baby
Feed refusal, fewer wet nappies, faltering growth; onset after 6 months
psychosocial: Sleep deprivation and support at home
Maternal mood — the two depression identification questions

playbook.diagnosis: Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux in a thriving infant with no red flags. Possible parental exhaustion or low mood needs its own follow-up.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The valve at the top of his tummy is still immature, so milk slips back up. He’s growing well, which tells me he’s getting plenty. Most babies grow out of it by their first birthday.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried he’s in pain and that you’re doing something wrong. You’re not — and the fact that he’s growing well is the best sign that he’s getting what he needs.”
management.psychosocial: Validate her exhaustion, screen her mood, arrange health-visitor support this week and a separate appointment for her; address the friend’s-baby comparison without judgement.
sharedPlan: Feeding review; smaller, more frequent feeds; thickened feed if formula and no improvement
Breastfeeding assessment if breastfed; alginate trial for 1 to 2 weeks only after these, never with a thickener
No PPI or H2 antagonist for regurgitation alone; back to sleep on a flat surface
safetyNet: 999: floppy, hard to wake, breathing difficulty. Same day: forceful or green vomit, blood, feed refusal, dry nappies, fever
Mother: contact us or 111 if she cannot cope or has thoughts of harm; review in two weeks

pitfalls.intro: Two patients are in this station. Candidates pass the baby and fail the mother, or satisfy the mother with a prescription that NICE NG1 advises against.

items.fail: Prescribing omeprazole or another acid-suppressing medicine because the mother is desperate.
items.why: NICE NG1 advises against acid suppression for overt regurgitation alone; “management not in line with UK guidance” is a Tasks fail.
items.fix: Explain why it will not help, then give the stepwise feeding plan and the conditions under which you would reconsider.

items.fail: Reassuring without checking growth or asking about projectile, green or bloody vomit.
items.why: Reassurance without assessment is unsafe; examiners expect the red flags and the growth trajectory.
items.fix: Ask the red-flag questions and look at the red-book weights before you say “normal”.

items.fail: Never asking how the mother is.
items.why: “I can’t keep doing this” is a cue; missing maternal mood is the commonest failing statement in this station.
items.fix: “Can I ask about you for a moment?” — then the two mood questions and a plan for her.

items.fail: Advising a thickener and Gaviscon together, or raising the cot.
items.why: NICE NG1 sequences these and advises against positional management in sleep.
items.fix: Feeds first, thickener if formula, then alginate alone; always back to sleep.

items.fail: Using clinical words — “GORD”, “alginate”, “pyloric stenosis” — without explaining them.
items.why: Unexplained jargon to an exhausted parent fails the Global Skills domain.
items.fix: “The valve at the top of his tummy”; “a feed thickener”; “forceful vomiting that shoots across the room”.

items.why: The mother’s risk is part of the case; a plan with no follow-up for her is incomplete.
items.fix: Health visitor this week, an appointment for her, and what to do if she feels she cannot cope.

wordPics.pass: Takes a feeding history, checks growth and red flags, explains normal reflux, gives NG1 feeding advice, avoids acid suppression and gives a safety-net.

avoid.instead: “It is very common, and he’s thriving — but I can see how hard it is for you, so let’s make a plan for both of you.”
avoid.why: Accurate reassurance delivered as dismissal fails the relating domain.

If he were refusing feeds, very distressed despite the other changes, or not growing, we’d think again.
SCA_MODELS.why: Declines the PPI with a clear reason and a conditional plan

SCA_MODELS.text: So there’s nothing?

There’s quite a lot. If he’s on bottles, we try smaller feeds more often, keeping the total the same, and if that doesn’t help, a thickened feed. If he’s breastfed, I’d like the health visitor or a feeding specialist to watch a feed. And if he stays very unsettled after that, a short trial of an alginate like Gaviscon Infant is reasonable — just not together with a thickener.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG1 stepwise plan for both feeding methods without inventing which applies

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That sounds more doable than I thought.
Good. We’ll start with the feed review and smaller, more frequent feeds. Keep putting him down to sleep on his back — raising the cot or sleeping him on his front isn’t safe and doesn’t help.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safe sleep advice; avoids positional treatment in sleep

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.

And for you: I’d like the health visitor to visit this week, and I’d like to see you — just you — in a couple of weeks to talk about how you’re sleeping and feeling. If you ever feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself or Alfie, call us or 111 straight away.
SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the mother as a patient too, with a specific safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: That would help. Thank you.

For Alfie, call 999 if he’s floppy, hard to wake or struggling to breathe. Contact us the same day if the vomit becomes forceful or green, there’s blood, he refuses feeds, has far fewer wet nappies, or has a fever. And bring him back if he stops following his growth line.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific red flags for obstruction, pyloric stenosis, dehydration and illness

SCA_MODELS.text: Forceful, green, blood, not feeding, dry nappies.

Exactly. So: it’s common reflux, he’s thriving, we adjust feeds rather than use acid medicine, the health visitor comes this week, and I see you in two weeks. Does that feel like a plan you can manage?
Yes. I feel a bit less like I’m failing him.

SCA_STEM.name: Alfie
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Video appointment booked by his mother: brings milk back after most feeds, cries and arches his back. Mother reports being up all night.
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother asking for “something to stop it”; a friend’s baby was prescribed a reflux medicine.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG1 (2015, updated 2019) — Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease in children and young people · NICE CG116 — Food allergy in under 19s · NICE CG192 — Antenatal and postnatal mental health · BNFC
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Regurgitation in a thriving, well baby is gastro-oesophageal reflux, not disease. Assess feeding, growth and red flags, then reassure and adjust feeds. Acid suppression is not for regurgitation alone. The exhausted parent is part of the consultation.

points.t: NICE NG1: regurgitation affects about 40% of infants, usually starts before 8 weeks, becomes less frequent with time and resolves in about 90% before 1 year. It does not usually need investigation or treatment.

points.h: Red flags that change the diagnosis
points.t: NICE NG1: bile-stained (green) or blood-stained vomit, projectile vomiting in the first 2 months (pyloric stenosis), abdominal distension, onset after 6 months, bulging fontanelle, fever or systemic illness, blood in the stool, faltering growth.

NICE NG1: review the feeding history; reduce volumes only if excessive for weight; try smaller, more frequent feeds with the same total daily amount; then a thickened formula; then stop the thickener and try an alginate for 1 to 2 weeks.
NICE NG1: a breastfeeding assessment by someone with the right training first; consider an alginate trial for 1 to 2 weeks if distress continues. Do not use a thickener and an alginate together.

NICE NG1: do not offer a PPI or H2 receptor antagonist for overt regurgitation alone. Consider a 4-week trial only with unexplained feeding difficulty, distressed behaviour or faltering growth, and stop it if there is no response. Do not advise positional management for sleeping infants — back to sleep.

NICE CG116: consider non-IgE-mediated cow’s milk allergy if there is eczema, diarrhoea or blood or mucus in the stool alongside reflux. NICE CG192: ask about the parent’s mood using the depression identification questions.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; noticed the exhausted parent on screen; let her describe the feeds, crying and back-arching.
Sleep deprivation, support at home, comparison with a friend’s baby, feeling of failing.
Picked up “I can’t keep doing this” and “I’m doing something wrong” and moved to the mother’s mood.
Idea (reflux needs medicine); concern (he is in pain, she is failing); expectation (a prescription).
Red-book weights plotted; observed on video; face-to-face review if any doubt; no investigations for uncomplicated reflux.
GOR versus GORD, pyloric stenosis, obstruction, cow’s milk allergy, infection and overfeeding.
Projectile, bilious or bloody vomit, feed refusal, hydration, fever, faltering growth, eczema or blood in stools.
Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux in a thriving infant; possible maternal exhaustion or low mood to explore.
NG1 stepwise feeding measures, alginate only after that and not with a thickener, no PPI for regurgitation alone, back-to-sleep advice.
Maternal mood screened with CG192 questions; health-visitor involvement; separate appointment for the mother.
999 and same-day features named; growth monitoring; review for the mother in two weeks; crisis advice.

social.t: Exhaustion reduces a parent’s ability to cope and raises risk; practical support at home and from the health visitor is part of the treatment.
Friends’ experiences and online forums drive requests for medicine; acknowledge them rather than dismiss them.

legal.t: A crying baby with an exhausted parent is a recognised risk situation for abusive head trauma. Ask about coping, give advice on what to do if overwhelmed, and act on any concern.

professional.t: NICE CG192: at contacts in the first postnatal year, consider asking the depression identification questions. Offer her a separate appointment and record the discussion.
Declining an unhelpful medicine while offering a clear alternative plan is good practice (GMC Good medical practice, 2024).

community.t: The health visitor can review feeding and growth and assess maternal wellbeing; infant-feeding specialists support breastfeeding assessment. Cry-sis offers a helpline for parents of crying babies.

redFlags: Projectile vomiting in the first 2 months (pyloric stenosis); bile-stained vomit (obstruction) — same-day surgical assessment
Blood in vomit or stool, distension, bulging fontanelle, fever or a floppy baby
Feed refusal, fewer wet nappies, faltering growth; onset after 6 months
psychosocial: Sleep deprivation and support at home
Maternal mood — the two depression identification questions
Feelings of failure and comparison with other parents
ice: Idea: “He has reflux and needs a medicine like my friend’s baby”
Concern: he is in pain; she is failing him

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux in a thriving infant with no red flags. Possible parental exhaustion or low mood needs its own follow-up.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The valve at the top of his tummy is still immature, so milk slips back up. He’s growing well, which tells me he’s getting plenty. Most babies grow out of it by their first birthday.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried he’s in pain and that you’re doing something wrong. You’re not — and the fact that he’s growing well is the best sign that he’s getting what he needs.”
management.psychosocial: Validate her exhaustion, screen her mood, arrange health-visitor support this week and a separate appointment for her; address the friend’s-baby comparison without judgement.
sharedPlan: Feeding review; smaller, more frequent feeds; thickened feed if formula and no improvement
Breastfeeding assessment if breastfed; alginate trial for 1 to 2 weeks only after these, never with a thickener
No PPI or H2 antagonist for regurgitation alone; back to sleep on a flat surface
safetyNet: 999: floppy, hard to wake, breathing difficulty. Same day: forceful or green vomit, blood, feed refusal, dry nappies, fever
Mother: contact us or 111 if she cannot cope or has thoughts of harm; review in two weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Two patients are in this station. Candidates pass the baby and fail the mother, or satisfy the mother with a prescription that NICE NG1 advises against.

items.fail: Prescribing omeprazole or another acid-suppressing medicine because the mother is desperate.
items.why: NICE NG1 advises against acid suppression for overt regurgitation alone; “management not in line with UK guidance” is a Tasks fail.
items.fix: Explain why it will not help, then give the stepwise feeding plan and the conditions under which you would reconsider.

items.fail: Reassuring without checking growth or asking about projectile, green or bloody vomit.
items.why: Reassurance without assessment is unsafe; examiners expect the red flags and the growth trajectory.
items.fix: Ask the red-flag questions and look at the red-book weights before you say “normal”.

items.fail: Never asking how the mother is.
items.why: “I can’t keep doing this” is a cue; missing maternal mood is the commonest failing statement in this station.
items.fix: “Can I ask about you for a moment?” — then the two mood questions and a plan for her.

items.fail: Advising a thickener and Gaviscon together, or raising the cot.
items.why: NICE NG1 sequences these and advises against positional management in sleep.
items.fix: Feeds first, thickener if formula, then alginate alone; always back to sleep.

items.fail: Using clinical words — “GORD”, “alginate”, “pyloric stenosis” — without explaining them.
items.why: Unexplained jargon to an exhausted parent fails the Global Skills domain.
items.fix: “The valve at the top of his tummy”; “a feed thickener”; “forceful vomiting that shoots across the room”.

items.why: The mother’s risk is part of the case; a plan with no follow-up for her is incomplete.
items.fix: Health visitor this week, an appointment for her, and what to do if she feels she cannot cope.
